title: Festival Gate Scanners
prompt: At a music festival, staff scan tickets at the gates with phones. Every scan asks the server to accept the ticket and mark it used. When the gates open, scans arrive faster than one server can handle. Design the server side.
facts: Peak: about 1,200 scans per second in the first 20 minutes
A load test shows one server reaches its limit at about 250 scans per second
At peak, each server must stay at or below 70% of its limit, even with one server down

Tickets are kept in one database that handles at least 3,000 writes per second. It offers one operation, "mark used if unused", that does the check and the mark together and answers accepted or already used, so a ticket is never accepted twice
If a scan gets no answer, the scanner sends it again; the database answers "accepted" again when the same scanner repeats a scan within one minute
scope: Selling tickets is out of scope

requirements: States the peak load, the 70% limit and the one-server-down requirement
States that every server uses the shared "mark used if unused" operation, so a ticket is accepted once
estimation: Per-server target: 250 × 0.7 = 175 scans per second; 1,200 ÷ 175 ≈ 6.9, so 7 working servers; with one down, run 8 (1,200 ÷ 7 ≈ 171 per server)
design: Scanners → load balancer (made redundant) → identical stateless servers → one shared database
Health checks remove a failed server from the load balancer
data: The servers keep no ticket state; the shared database decides whether a ticket is used, so any server can take any scan
Notes the database's 3,000 writes per second covers 1,200 scans per second
tradeoffs: Names a trade-off with its condition, such as: checking every 5 s with 2 failed checks means up to about 10 s of scans sent to a dead server, which the scanner repeats safely; or the load balancer must be redundant, or it becomes the single point of failure; or a hardware load balancer versus a managed one

fullMarkDesigns: Design A: an active and a standby load balancer send scans round robin to 8 stateless servers; each server calls "mark used if unused" in the shared database. 1,200 ÷ 175 ≈ 6.9 → 7 servers, plus 1 so one can fail. Health checks every 2 s, 2 failures to remove: up to about 4 s of scans to a dead server, which scanners repeat safely.

Design B: a managed load balancer that sends each scan to the server with the fewest open requests (least connections), and 9 servers chosen for more room: 1,200 ÷ 8 = 150 per server with one down, 60% of the limit. Same stateless servers and database operation. Trade-off: one more server costs money but leaves room if the gates open faster than planned.

assumptions: Scans are spread evenly by the load balancer
The database stays fast at 1,200 writes per second
reference.design:
Scanner phones send each scan to a redundant pair of load balancers, which spread scans across identical stateless servers. Each server calls the database's "mark used if unused" operation, which accepts a ticket once.
Server count: at 70% of 250, one server takes 175 scans per second; 1,200 ÷ 175 ≈ 6.9, so 7 servers are needed. Running 8 keeps the 70% limit when one is down: 1,200 ÷ 7 ≈ 171 per server.
Health checks remove a failed server within seconds; scans sent to it in that time get no answer, and scanners repeat them safely.
alternatives: One very large server (vertical scaling): simpler, but a single point of failure at the gates
Sticky routing of each scanner to one server: not needed, because the servers keep no state

title: Logged Out at Random
prompt: A homework portal keeps each student's login session in the memory of the server that handled the login. The team added a second server behind a round-robin load balancer, and students now get logged out at random. Design how sessions should work.
facts: 30,000 students; each session holds about 1 KB and lasts up to 7 days
Peak traffic: about 400 requests per second across 2 servers, each request needing the student's session
A student must stay logged in when either server is restarted for an update, and when servers are added
Available: a shared in-memory store that handles about 50,000 lookups per second and can keep a copy (replica) on a second machine
Also possible: the server signs a small token (about 300 bytes) with the student id and expiry, which any server can check without a lookup; checking a signature takes well under 1 ms
scope: Keeping students logged in across servers
How students first log in is out of scope

requirements: Explains why students are logged out: the next request may go to the server that does not hold the session
States the requirement that sessions survive a restart of any one server and adding servers
estimation: For a shared store: 30,000 × 1 KB = 30 MB of sessions and 400 lookups per second against 50,000
Or for signed tokens: 400 checks per second at under 1 ms each, and about 300 bytes more per request
design: Stateless servers behind the load balancer, with sessions in one shared store, or a signed token kept by the browser
Any server can serve any request
data: Says where the session lives and how a server finds it (session id in a cookie, then a lookup), or what the signed token contains and how it is checked
tradeoffs: Explains why sticky sessions alone break the requirement: a restarted server loses its students' sessions

Names one trade-off of the chosen design with its condition, such as: the shared store needs its replica or one failure logs everyone out; a signed token cannot be cancelled before it expires without shared revocation data

fullMarkDesigns: Design A: sessions move to the shared in-memory store with its replica; the browser's cookie holds only the session id, and each server looks the session up. 30,000 × 1 KB = 30 MB, and 400 lookups per second against 50,000. Restarts and new servers log no one out. Trade-off: without the replica, one store failure would log everyone out.

Design B: the server signs a token with the student id and a 1-day expiry; the browser sends it with each request and any server checks the signature: 400 checks per second at under 1 ms, about 300 bytes extra per request, no store at all. Trade-off: a token cannot be cancelled early without shared revocation data, so the expiry is kept short and students log in again daily.

assumptions: The load balancer stays round robin
The shared store is in the same data center as the servers
reference.design:
The servers become stateless. At login, the server stores the session (about 1 KB) in the shared in-memory store and sets a cookie with only the session id. Every request, on either server, reads the session from the store.
Size and load: 30,000 × 1 KB = 30 MB, and 400 lookups per second against the store's 50,000.
Restarting one server or adding servers logs no one out, because no server keeps sessions in its own memory. The store keeps its replica so that one failure does not log everyone out.
alternatives: Sticky sessions: quick fix for the random logouts, but a restart still logs out that server's students and load becomes uneven
Signed tokens: no store, but cancelling a session early needs shared revocation data
